plan.topic_summary: Silicon photonics integrates optical components (waveguides, modulators, detectors, and potentially lasers) on silicon substrates to enable high-bandwidth, low-power interconnects. For a 1–5 year view, the central question is how quickly it can displace or complement electrical interconnects in AI data centers and chip-to-chip links, and what manufacturing, packaging, and cost barriers must be cleared.
key_questions: What is the current state of co-packaged optics (CPO) deployments in hyperscale data centers, and which foundries are qualified for silicon photonics production at scale?
What are the current cost-per-channel and power-per-bit figures for silicon photonics versus copper interconnects, and at what scale does the economic crossover occur?
How quickly can III-V laser integration on silicon achieve the reliability and yield needed for mass production, and what are the main technical bottlenecks?
What is the realistic timeline for silicon photonics to extend from data center interconnects to chip-to-chip and on-chip communication?
What supply chain constraints (specialty equipment, III-V epitaxy, advanced packaging) could limit scaling of silicon photonics over the next 3–5 years?

gaps: No dedicated finding quantifying state-of-the-art silicon modulator bandwidth in GHz; S6 gives a system-level 512 Gb/s over 32 channels but per-channel modulator bandwidth is not explicitly extracted.
No specific foundry yield data; R3 discusses fabrication variation qualitatively but no yield percentages or defect-density numbers are cited.

CPO-specific technical challenges (power budget, thermal management within the package, serviceability trade-offs) are well-covered by patents (P1-P3) and market filings (M1, M3) but lack a dedicated science finding from the peer-reviewed literature.
Cost-per-channel evidence is thin: only the UMC 7x-CMOS price point from a social signal (X1) and no peer-reviewed or filing-based cost breakdown.
Reliability and long-term degradation data are acknowledged as a gap in R2 ('only extrapolated, not measured') but no quantitative lifetime or degradation-rate data is available.
M9 notes that major AI-accelerator and foundry companies (NVIDIA, Intel, Broadcom, TSMC) did not appear in retrieved filing excerpts, so their silicon photonics positions are uncharacterized.

sources.title: Roadmapping the next generation of silicon photonics
sources.abstract: Silicon photonics has developed into a mainstream technology driven by advances in optical communications. The current generation has led to a proliferation of integrated photonic devices from thousands to millions-mainly in the form of communication transceivers for data centers. Products in many exciting applications, such as sensing and computing, are around the corner. What will it take to increase the proliferation of silicon photonics from millions to billions of units shipped? What will the next generation of silicon photonics look like? What are the common threads in the integration and fabrication bottlenecks that silicon photonic applications face, and which emerging technologies can solve them? This perspective article is an attempt to answer such questions. We chart the generational trends in silicon photonics technology, drawing parallels from the generational definitions of CMOS technology. We identify the crucial challenges that must be solved to make giant strides in CMOS-foundry-compatible devices, circuits, integration, and packaging. We identify challenges critical to the next generation of systems and applications-in communication, signal processing, and sensing. By identifying and summarizing such challenges and opportunities, we aim to stimulate further research on devices, circuits, and systems for the silicon photonics ecosystem.

sources.title: Integrated silicon photonic MEMS
affiliations: Swiss Center for Electronics and Microtechnology (Switzerland)
sources.abstract: Silicon photonics has emerged as a mature technology that is expected to play a key role in critical emerging applications, including very high data rate optical communications, distance sensing for autonomous vehicles, photonic-accelerated computing, and quantum information processing. The success of silicon photonics has been enabled by the unique combination of performance, high yield, and high-volume capacity that can only be achieved by standardizing manufacturing technology. Today, standardized silicon photonics technology platforms implemented by foundries provide access to optimized library components, including low-loss optical routing, fast modulation, continuous tuning, high-speed germanium photodiodes, and high-efficiency optical and electrical interfaces. However, silicon's relatively weak electro-optic effects result in modulators with a significant footprint and thermo-optic tuning devices that require high power consumption, which are substantial impediments for very large-scale integration in silicon photonics. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) technology can enhance silicon photonics with building blocks that are compact, low-loss, broadband, fast and require very low power consumption. Here, we introduce a silicon photonic MEMS platform consisting of high-performance nano-opto-electromechanical devices fully integrated alongside standard silicon photonics foundry components, with wafer-level sealing for long-term reliability, flip-chip bonding to redistribution interposers, and fibre-array attachment for high port count optical and electrical interfacing. Our experimental demonstration of fundamental silicon photonic MEMS circuit elements, including power couplers, phase shifters and wavelength-division multiplexing devices using standardized technology lifts previous impediments to enable scaling to very large photonic integrated circuits for applications in telecommunications, neuromorphic computing, sensing, programmable photonics, and quantum computing.

sources.title: A high-speed heterogeneous lithium tantalate silicon photonics platform
sources.abstract: The rapid expansion of cloud computing and artificial intelligence has driven the demand for faster optical components in data centres to unprecedented levels. A key advancement in this field is the integration of multiple photonic components onto a single chip, enhancing the performance of optical transceivers. Here, silicon photonics, benefiting from mature fabrication processes, has gained prominence. The platform combines modulators, switches, photodetectors and low-loss waveguides on a single chip. However, emerging standards like 1600ZR+ potentially exceed the capabilities of silicon-based modulators. To address these limitations, thin-film lithium niobate has been proposed as an alternative to silicon photonics, offering a low voltage-length product and exceptional high-speed modulation properties. More recently, the first demonstrations of thin-film lithium tantalate circuits have emerged, addressing some of the disadvantages of lithium niobate enabling a reduced bias drift and enhanced resistance to optical damage. As such, making it a promising candidate for next-generation photonic platforms. However, a persistent drawback of such platforms is the lithium contamination, which complicates integration with CMOS fabrication processes. Here, we present for the first time the integration of lithium tantalate onto a silicon photonics chip. This integration is achieved without modifying the standard silicon photonics process design kit. Our device achieves low half-wave voltage (3.5 V), low insertion loss (2.9 dB) and high-speed operation (> 70 GHz), paving the way for next-gen applications. By minimising lithium tantalate material use, our approach reduces costs while leveraging existing silicon photonics technology advancements, in particular supporting ultra-fast monolithic germanium photodetectors and established process design kits.

sources.title: Silicon photonics for the visible and near-infrared spectrum
sources.abstract: Emerging applications in quantum information, microscopy, biosensing, depth sensing, and augmented reality demand miniaturized components in the visible (VIS) and near-infrared (NIR) spectrum with wavelengths between 380 and 1100 nm. Foundry silicon photonics, which has been optimized for telecommunication wavelengths, can be adapted to this wavelength range. In this article, we review recent developments in silicon photonics for VIS and NIR wavelengths, with a focus on platforms, devices, and photonic circuits fabricated in foundries. Foundries enable the creation of complex circuitry at a wafer scale. Platforms based on silicon nitride and aluminum oxide wave-guides compatible with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) foundries are becoming available. As a result, highly functional photonic circuits are becoming possible. The key challenges are low-loss waveguides, efficient input/output coupling, sensitive detectors, and heterogeneous integration of lasers and modulators, particularly those using lithium niobate and other electro-optic materials. These elements, already developed for telecommunications, require further development for λ < 1100 nm. As short-wavelength silicon photonics technology advances, photonic integrated circuits can address a broader scope of applications beyond O- and C-band communication.

sources.title: Zero-change foundry compatible silicon photonics MEMS optical switch
sources.abstract: Large-scale photonic switches are emerging as essential devices for energy-efficient optical interconnect in data centers and AI/ML clusters as a key enabler for high-bandwidth and low-latency connectivity. Combining micro-electro-mechanical (MEMS) based mechanical reconfigurability with silicon photonic integrated circuits can enable a large-scale, low-loss, programmable platform required for large-scale optical circuit switches. We demonstrate a broadband silicon photonics MEMS switch with more than 30 dB extinction ratio operating in C-band using a zero-change foundry-compatible process and Back-end-of-Line (BEOL) post-processing. The optical switch element exhibits an insertion loss of less than 1.5 dB with a low static power consumption of approx 20 nW at maximum actuation voltage. Our results illustrate that MEMS-based silicon photonics modulators and phase shifters can be used alongside standard silicon photonics components seamlessly in scenarios where performance in terms of footprint, extinction ratio, broad bandwidth, and low-loss operation is of paramount importance.

sources.title: Silicon Photonics
sources.abstract: Complete coverage of the field of silicon-based photonic devices, including a chapter on nonlinear silicon photonics Silicon Photonics discusses the physics, technology, and device operation of photonic devices using silicon, Group IV semiconductors, and their alloys. The book delivers an optimal combination of background information about photonic structures with description of up-to-date results and trends in silicon photonics. This Second Edition includes a new chapter on nonlinear silicon photonics as well as numerous updates to existing content. Readers will find information on the role of silicon in photonics and its advantages and disadvantages as well as the properties of these alloys. Subsequent chapters in Silicon Photonics explore topics including: Quantum structures, covering quantum wells, wires, and dots, superlattices, Si-based quantum structures, and effects of electric fields Optical processes, covering absorption processes in semiconductors, intervalence band absorption, free-carrier absorption, and recombination and luminescence Si light modulators, covering electrorefraction, thermo-optic effects, modulators, and optical and electrical structures Raman lasers, covering Raman scattering, the Raman effect in silicon, the Raman gain coefficient, and continuous-wave Raman lasers Principles of planar waveguide devices, covering directional couplers and distributed Bragg reflectors Fabrication technologies and material systems Silicon Photonics is an excellent resource on the subject for electrical engineers, applied physicists, materials scientists, and senior undergraduate and postgraduate students working in Si photonics and related fields. This significantly rewritten book includes a new chapter on nonlinear silicon photonics as well as numerous updates to existing content compared to the earlier textbook.

sources.title: Entanglement Purification by Integrated Silicon Photonics
sources.abstract: We demonstrate the first on-chip deterministic entanglement purification based on silicon photonics. To evaluate the purification performance, we simulate the bit-flip and phase-flip errors by reconfigurable circuits on chip. The state fidelity improves from 0.71 to 0.82 under a 20% bit-flip error. rate

sources.title: Silicon photonics for high-speed communications and photonic signal processing
sources.abstract: Abstract Leveraging on the mature processing infrastructure of silicon microelectronics, silicon photonic integrated circuits may be readily scaled to large volume production for low-cost high-volume applications such as optical transceivers for data centers. Driven by the rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence and the resultant rapid increase in data traffic in data centers, new integrated optical transceivers will be needed to support multichannel high-capacity communications beyond 1.6Tb/s. In this paper, we review some of the recent advances in high performance optical waveguide grating couplers (WGC) as a key enabling technology for future high capacity communications. We describe the novel use of shifted-polysilicon overlay gratings on top of the silicon grating that enabled foundry manufactured chips to have fiber-chip coupling losses of under 1 dB. The use of mirror symmetry and resonant cavity enhancement in the design of gratings can increase the 1-dB optical bandwidths of grating couplers to over 100 nm. Multimode waveguide grating couplers (MWGC) may be designed for the selective launch of different modes channels in multimode fibers for mode-division-multiplexing (MDM) communications. The use of different modes or polarizations in optical fibers for high capacity communications requires the unscrambling of data lanes which are mixed together during the optical fiber transmission. We describe how silicon photonic circuits can be used to perform unitary matrix operations and unscramble the different data lanes in multichannel optical communication systems. We also describe recent advances on high-speed silicon modulators for enabling data rates of individual data lanes in an integrated optical transceiver beyond 300 Gb/s.

sources.title: Calibration of cascaded phase shifters using pairwise scan method in silicon photonics integrated chip
sources.abstract: Cascaded phase shifters (CPSs) based on silicon photonics integrated chips play important roles in quantum information processing tasks. Owing to an increase in the scale of silicon photonics chips, the time required to calibrate various CPSs has increased. We propose a pairwise scan method for rapidly calibrating CPSs by introducing equivalent Mach Zehnder Interferometer structures and a reasonable constraint of the initial relative phase. The calibration can be nearly completed when the scanning process is finished, and only a little calculation is required. To achieve better performance, the key components, thermal optical phase shifter and 2 * 2 50/50 multimode interference coupler, were simulated and optimized to prevent thermal crosstalk and ensure a good balance. A 6-CPSs structure in a packaged silicon photonics chip under different temperature was used to verify the rapid pairwise scan method, and a fidelity of 99.97% was achieved.

sources.title: The Intelligent Design of Silicon Photonic Devices
sources.abstract: Abstract Photonic devices based on silicon waveguides are essential to versatile high‐performance and low‐cost photonic integrated systems. Extremely complex silicon photonic devices with hundreds or even thousands of degrees of freedom (DOF) are successfully designed and manufactured based on recent advances in data science and nanofabrication technology. At this level, conventional forward‐reasoning may no longer be suitable for designing high‐performance silicon photonic devices with novel functionalities since the light‐matter interaction is complex and non‐intuitive. Therefore, the timely development of sub‐wavelength silicon photonic devices that can precisely mold the flow of light is a critical and urgent issue requiring joint engineering and scientific efforts. In this paper, an inverse design strategy based on heuristic and gradient descendant algorithms, enabling the realization of large‐scale integrated devices is first introduced. Subsequently, the burgeoning deep learning technology, which offers a promising direction for the automation design of silicon photonics with a data‐driven approach, is discussed. Finally, the obstacles and prospects in this emerging research direction are revealed. Detail discussions from multiple perspectives are provided. This review aims to provide general guidance and a comprehensive reference for scientists developing photonic integrated systems.

sources.title: A silicon photonics waveguide-coupled colloidal quantum dot photodiode sensitive beyond 1.6 um
sources.abstract: Silicon photonics faces a persistent challenge in extending photodetection capabilities beyond the 1.6 um wavelength range, primarily due to the lack of appropriate epitaxial materials. Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) present a promising solution here, offering distinct advantages such as infrared wavelength tunability, cost-effectiveness, and facile deposition. Their unique properties position them as a potential candidate for enabling photodetection in silicon photonics beyond the conventional telecom wavelength, thereby expanding the potential applications and capabilities within this domain. In this study, we have successfully integrated lead sulfide (PbS) colloidal quantum dot photodiodes (QDPDs) onto silicon waveguides using standard process techniques. The integrated photodiodes exhibit a remarkable responsivity of 1.3 A/W (with an external quantum efficiency of 74.8%) at a wavelength of 2.1 um, a low dark current of only 106 nA and a bandwidth of 1.1 MHz under a -3 V bias. To demonstrate the scalability of our integration approach, we have developed a compact 8-channel spectrometer incorporating an array of QDPDs. This achievement marks a significant step toward realizing a cost-effective photodetector solution for silicon photonics, particularly tailored for a wide range of sensing applications around the 2 um wavelength range.

sources.title: Massively scalable Kerr comb-driven silicon photonic link
sources.abstract: Abstract The growth of computing needs for artificial intelligence and machine learning is critically challenging data communications in today’s data-centre systems. Data movement, dominated by energy costs and limited ‘chip-escape’ bandwidth densities, is perhaps the singular factor determining the scalability of future systems. Using light to send information between compute nodes in such systems can dramatically increase the available bandwidth while simultaneously decreasing energy consumption. Through wavelength-division multiplexing with chip-based microresonator Kerr frequency combs, independent information channels can be encoded onto many distinct colours of light in the same optical fibre for massively parallel data transmission with low energy. Although previous high-bandwidth demonstrations have relied on benchtop equipment for filtering and modulating Kerr comb wavelength channels, data-centre interconnects require a compact on-chip form factor for these operations. Here we demonstrate a massively scalable chip-based silicon photonic data link using a Kerr comb source enabled by a new link architecture and experimentally show aggregate single-fibre data transmission of 512 Gb s−1 across 32 independent wavelength channels. The demonstrated architecture is fundamentally scalable to hundreds of wavelength channels, enabling massively parallel terabit-scale optical interconnects for future green hyperscale data centres.

sources.title: Polarization management in silicon photonics
sources.abstract: Abstract Polarization management plays a key role in various applications, such as optical communications, imaging, and sensing. It not only mitigates detrimental effects (e.g., polarization mode dispersion in optical communication) but also enables advanced functionalities, such as polarization multiplexing and optical isolation. Herein, we review the state-of-the-art approaches for on-chip polarization management. Additionally, we discuss strategies for developing non-reciprocal photonic devices and the challenges associated with monolithic integration in photonics circuits.

sources.title: Modelling Fabrication Variability in Silicon Photonic Devices
sources.abstract: Silicon photonics allows for high yield and complex integration with large processing, packaging, and testing availability. Using silicon as a material leverages the use of the existing CMOS infrastructure with hybrid and epitaxial layer integration, allowing photonic system-on-chip. Although high refractive index contrast with sub micrometer waveguide dimensions allows a dense integration, sensitivity to fabrication variations shows an increased effect. This sensitivity shows a cumulative effect on the optical properties of complex silicon photonic circuits such as lattice filters, and wavelength division multiplexers (WDM). This increases the demand for model fabrication variation at the design stage itself since the fabless users have no insights into the process specifications. As a result, reliability modelling of photonic circuits has shown significant interest in recent years. This is done by using efficient behavioural models at the circuit level and then applying random variations in the model parameters to assess the impact of these variations. In this chapter, different approaches to modelling fabrication variations in photonic integrated circuits, such as Monte Carlo (MC), Stochastic Collocation (SC), and Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE) are reviewed. These methods employ random distribution to the varying parameters with the correlation between different parameter sets fixed. Virtual Wafer-based MC (VW-MC) allows layout-aware variability analysis, where the placement of circuit components on the layout coordinates is exported to the circuit design for dependence analysis. Using these methods, mitigation strategies to counter the manufacturing variations such as thermal compensation, and tapered designs are quantitatively evaluated by appropriate yield analysis and design for manufacturability.

sources.title: Photonic millimeter-wave generation beyond the cavity thermal limit
sources.abstract: Next-generation communications, radar, and navigation systems will extend and exploit the higher bandwidth of the millimeter-wave domain for increased communication data rates as well as radar with higher sensitivity and increased spatial resolution. However, realizing these advantages will require the generation of millimeter-wave signals with low phase noise in simple and compact form-factors. Photonic integration addresses this challenge and provides a path toward simplified and portable, low-noise mm-wave generation. We leverage these advances by heterodyning two silicon photonic chip lasers, phase-locked to different axial modes of a miniature Fabry–Perot (F-P) cavity to demonstrate a simple framework for generating low-noise millimeter-waves. By reducing technical noise, we achieve common-mode rejection of the thermally driven Brownian noise such that the millimeter-wave phase noise surpasses that of the thermal limit of a single laser locked to the F-P cavity. This leads to a 118.1 GHz millimeter-wave signal with phase noise of −118dBc/Hz at 10 kHz offset, decreasing to −120dBc/Hz at 30 kHz offset. We achieve this with technologies that can be integrated into a platform less than ≈10mL. Our work overcomes fundamental thermal-mechanical noise limits intrinsic to integrated photonics, while illustrating advantages of the same for providing low-size, -weight, and -power (SWaP) mm-waves that will be enabling for multiple applications in communications and sensing.

sources.title: On-Chip Lasers for Silicon Photonics
sources.abstract: With the growing trend in the information industry, silicon photonics technology has been explored in both academia and industry and utilized for high-bandwidth data transmission. Thanks to the benefits of silicon, such as high refractive index contrast with its oxides, low loss, substantial thermal–optical effect, and compatibility with CMOS, a range of passive and active photonic devices have been demonstrated, including waveguides, modulators, photodetectors, and lasers. The most challenging aspect remains to be the on-chip laser source, whose performance is constrained by the indirect bandgap of silicon. This review paper highlights the advancements made in the field of integrated laser sources on the silicon photonics platform. These on-chip lasers are classified according to their gain media, including V semiconductors, III–V semiconductors, two-dimensional materials, and colloidal quantum dots. The methods of integrating these lasers onto silicon are also detailed in this review.

sources.title: Silicon integrated photonics
sources.abstract: Technologies of silicon integrated photonics are the basis for the fabrication of a class of devices, such as optical modulators, photodetectors, optical filters and switches, multiplexers and demultiplexers, and optical transceivers.In many respects, silicon integrated photonics competes with alternative platforms based on indium phosphide, silicon nitride and dioxide, and other platforms.Here we provide an overview of modern approaches used in silicon integrated photonic technologies, describe the components of photonic integrated circuits and devices developed on their basis, and make a comparison with alternative technology platforms.

sources.title: Multifunctionality in Silicon Photonics Through Temperature‐Driven Inverse Design
sources.abstract: ABSTRACT The scalability of programmable photonic systems relies on compact, low‐loss, and reconfigurable building blocks capable of supporting multiple optical functions. While silicon photonics offers several tunability mechanisms, many existing approaches rely on resonant architectures, extended interferometric paths, or heterogeneous functional materials that increase footprint, sensitivity, or process complexity. Here, a temperature‐dependent co‐optimization framework is applied that embeds thermal reconfigurability directly into the inverse‐design process, enabling multiple optical functionalities within a single device geometry. Using adjoint‐based topology optimization together with the intrinsic thermo‐optic response of silicon, a compact optical switch with a µm 2 footprint and a reconfigurable TE 0 –TE 2 mode converter occupying µm 2 have been designed as representative devices and experimentally verified. Both devices exhibit low insertion loss, < 2 dB, and clear thermally programmable behavior, with good agreement between numerical and experimental results. This approach establishes a general, CMOS‐compatible route toward dense, multifunctional programmable photonic circuits.

sources.title: 3D integration enables ultralow-noise isolator-free lasers in silicon photonics
sources.abstract: , photonic integrated circuits are still considered inferior solutions despite their advantages in size, weight, power consumption and cost. Such high-precision and highly coherent applications favour ultralow-noise laser sources to be integrated with other photonic components in a compact and robustly aligned format-that is, on a single chip-for photonic integrated circuits to replace bulk optics and fibres. There are two major issues preventing the realization of such envisioned photonic integrated circuits: the high phase noise of semiconductor lasers and the difficulty of integrating optical isolators directly on-chip. Here we challenge this convention by leveraging three-dimensional integration that results in ultralow-noise lasers with isolator-free operation for silicon photonics. Through multiple monolithic and heterogeneous processing sequences, direct on-chip integration of III-V gain medium and ultralow-loss silicon nitride waveguides with optical loss around 0.5 decibels per metre are demonstrated. Consequently, the demonstrated photonic integrated circuit enters a regime that gives rise to ultralow-noise lasers and microwave synthesizers without the need for optical isolators, owing to the ultrahigh-quality-factor cavity. Such photonic integrated circuits also offer superior scalability for complex functionalities and volume production, as well as improved stability and reliability over time. The three-dimensional integration on ultralow-loss photonic integrated circuits thus marks a critical step towards complex systems and networks on silicon.

sources.title: Silicon photonics as a platform for the sensorization of composite aerostructure production
sources.venue: International Conference on Optical Fiber Sensors (OFS)
sources.abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced composites are widely used in aerospace due to their low weight and high mechanical strength. Resin Transfer Molding (RTM) offers a cost-effective alternative to autoclave-based manufacturing but requires strict control over process parameters. Accurate monitoring of temperature, pressure, and the resin’s refractive index—key to assessing cure state—is essential for ensuring quality. This study introduces the first application of silicon photonic sensors in composite part manufacturing, leveraging their electrical passivity and thermal stability. Embedded in a multi-ton composite tool, the sensors—with a high thermo-optic sensitivity of 78.4 pm/°C and a linearity of 0.9787—operated under demanding RTM-6 conditions (up to 165 °C and 7 bar over six hours). Across the full temperature range (30–165 °C), they exhibited exceptional stability, enabling precise cure-state monitoring.

sources.title: Thermal flux manipulation on the silicon photonic chip to suppress the thermal crosstalk
sources.abstract: The integration density of silicon photonic integrated circuit (PIC) is ultimately constrained by various crosstalk mechanisms on the chip. Among them, the most prominent limiting factor is the thermal crosstalk due to the wide use of the thermo-optic effect. High-density silicon PICs strongly demand an advanced structure with better thermal crosstalk suppression ability than the traditional air isolation trench. Inspired by the thermal-metamaterial based on the scattering-cancellation method, we demonstrate a closed heat shield (CHS) structure on a silicon PIC chip, which can manipulate the thermal flux to bypass the temperature-sensitive silicon photonics components. The on-chip CHS structure is a bilayer cylindrical shell fabricated by the standard silicon photonics processing flow. Its outer and inner shell layers are formed by a 6-μm-wide interconnection metal and 4-μm-wide air trench, respectively. Plenty of temperature-sensitive micro-ring resonators inside the CHS are used to probe the temperature profile. The measurement results show that the CHS can reduce the local temperatures by 50%/44%/36% at the locations 29/41/83 μm away from the external heater. In contrast, the conventional air trench of the same dimension reduces the local temperatures by 32%/28%/21% at the same positions. In addition, the response time of the thermal field inside the CHS is around one-half of that in the conventional air trench. Furthermore, the simulation result indicates that if the outer shell of the CHS can contact with the silicon substrate by utilizing the through-silicon-via structure, the thermal crosstalk suppression ability can be improved significantly.

sources.title: In situ thermal trimming of waveguides in a standard active silicon photonics platform
sources.abstract: We present suspended heater structures fabricated in a standard C- and O-band silicon (Si) photonics platform that can achieve sufficiently high local temperatures to induce effective refractive index trimming of Si and silicon nitride (SiN) waveguides with 30 - 90 mW of applied electrical power. Following thermal trimming at moderate powers (≤40 mW), maximum changes in the averaged waveguide effective refractive index of −5.18 × 10 −3 and −7.9 × 10 −4 are demonstrated in SiN and Si waveguides, respectively, at a wavelength of 1550 nm. At higher powers, SiN waveguides exhibit positive averaged effective index changes up to ≈0.02, demonstrating bi-directional index trimming. As an example application, we demonstrate bias point trimming of a carrier injection Mach-Zehnder switch. Through investigations of the origin of the thermal trimming effect, we hypothesize that changes in the silica (SiO 2 ) waveguide cladding may be a primary underlying mechanism at temperatures ≳300°C, with significant trimming of SiN waveguide cores occurring at larger temperatures ≳510°C. As the trimming experiments represent a form of accelerated thermal aging, we estimate the aging behavior of the suspended heaters by fitting and extrapolating the measured datasets to 100 - 200°C operating temperatures over five years.

findings.claim: The on-chip laser remains the most challenging component of silicon photonics because silicon's indirect bandgap limits its performance. Light sources therefore depend on III-V or other heterogeneous integration, which adds process complexity.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This comes from a single review abstract. Its framing of the laser as the hardest part is consistent with the integration challenges raised in src_907edb4a60. The abstract does not quantify cost or yield penalties.
findings.supporting_excerpt: The most challenging aspect remains to be the on-chip laser source, whose performance is constrained by the indirect bandgap of silicon.

findings.claim: Thermal effects constrain density and stability. Thermal crosstalk from thermo-optic tuning is described as the most prominent limit on PIC integration density. Trimming heaters operating at high temperature raise long-term aging questions that are only extrapolated, not measured.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_3837ca0846 states that thermal crosstalk is the most prominent limiting factor on integration density. The crosstalk mitigation it demonstrates (a closed heat shield) reduces local temperature by up to 50%, so it leaves residual crosstalk. src_c3599d220d reports trimming effects that may arise from cladding changes at temperatures above about 300°C, and its five-year aging figures are fitted and extrapolated from accelerated data. src_bc726db42d builds reconfigurability on the thermo-optic response, so designs that rely on it inherit these thermal limits. The abstracts do not report power budgets at system scale. The papers are small device-level studies.

findings.claim: Fabrication variation is a structural risk for complex circuits. High index contrast and sub-micrometer waveguides make circuits such as WDM filters and lattice filters sensitive to process variation. Fabless users also lack insight into process specifications, so they must rely on statistical modelling.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This rests on one book chapter abstract that reviews modelling methods. The same abstract also says silicon photonics allows high yield, so the evidence is mixed and carries no actual yield data. The need for post-fabrication trimming (src_c3599d220d) is consistent with residual variation, but that is my inference.
findings.supporting_excerpt: sensitivity to fabrication variations shows an increased effect. This sensitivity shows a cumulative effect on the optical properties of complex silicon photonic circuits such as lattice filters, and wavelength division multiplexers (WDM).

findings.claim: Scaling from millions to billions of units is unproven. A highly cited roadmap says that integration, fabrication and packaging bottlenecks must be solved before volume can grow by orders of magnitude. Current volume is mainly data-center transceivers, and sensing and computing products are only 'around the corner'.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The roadmap is a perspective article, not an empirical study. It frames billions of units as a question and identifies crucial challenges in devices, circuits, integration and packaging. The abstract does not rank these challenges or give timelines.

findings.claim: Demonstrations of the key ideas for AI interconnects and low-noise lasers are laboratory-scale. The Kerr comb link reached 512 Gb/s over 32 channels, and the claim that it scales to hundreds of channels is stated as 'fundamentally scalable' rather than shown. The 3D-integrated low-noise laser relies on multiple monolithic and heterogeneous processing sequences, which implies manufacturing complexity.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Two abstracts only. The Kerr comb abstract does not discuss comb pump power, wavelength-locking overhead, link margin or cost against pluggable transceivers. The 3D integration abstract (truncated) does not address yield or cost. Calling manufacturing complex is my reading of 'multiple monolithic and heterogeneous processing sequences', not a stated result. Absence of this data is a gap, not proof of failure.

findings.claim: Silicon photonics competes with indium phosphide, silicon nitride and other platforms, and the low-noise results in these papers depend on silicon nitride waveguides and III-V gain. Silicon alone is therefore not sufficient for demanding functions, and the winning platform may be hybrid or non-silicon.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_b1ca6c716a says silicon integrated photonics competes with alternative platforms, but gives no comparison results in its abstract. src_907edb4a60 reaches ultralow noise by adding III-V gain and ultralow-loss SiN, and src_32bfe37076 notes thermal-mechanical noise limits intrinsic to integrated photonics, which it overcomes only through common-mode rejection with an external F-P cavity. The displacement conclusion is my inference.

findings.claim: Polarization management and the lack of easy on-chip non-reciprocal elements remain unsolved integration issues. Isolators are cited as hard to integrate directly on-chip, and the review flags challenges with monolithic integration.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_f2cd625a33 only mentions challenges associated with monolithic integration, without details. src_907edb4a60 states that integrating optical isolators on-chip is difficult. Their combined weight is modest.

findings.claim: Evidence for non-datacom applications such as sensing and composites monitoring is early. The aerostructure study is a conference paper that describes itself as a first application of silicon photonic sensors in composite part manufacturing, and it reports no comparison to incumbent fiber sensors or cost data.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This is a single conference abstract. It reports a thermo-optic sensitivity of 78.4 pm/°C and good stability up to 165 °C, but no sample counts, repeatability or commercial economics. This is a gap, not a negative result.

hype_flags: 'Millions to billions of units' – the roadmap poses this as a question and lists unresolved bottlenecks; no demand or cost evidence is provided.
'Fundamentally scalable to hundreds of wavelength channels' – this is a design claim, demonstrated at 32 channels.
'Sensing and computing around the corner' – the cited evidence consists of early-stage demonstrations.
'Beyond the thermal limit' mm-wave generation – the result uses a Fabry-Perot cavity setup and is a lab demonstration, not a product-level result.

finding.claim: S5 says silicon photonics platforms are being adapted to 380-1100 nm. The cited abstract says the foundry platforms becoming available for this range are based on silicon nitride and aluminum oxide waveguides, not silicon. Silicon absorbs strongly below about 1.1 µm. S5 therefore blurs a material-platform shift into 'silicon photonics extending its reach', which overstates the case for silicon itself.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract's own wording shows the visible/NIR capability comes from non-silicon waveguide materials in CMOS foundries. Whether this counts as 'silicon photonics' is a framing choice that the finding does not flag.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Platforms based on silicon nitride and aluminum oxide wave-guides compatible with complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) foundries are becoming available.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 presents the Kerr-comb link as a response to transceiver targets beyond 1.6 Tb/s. The demonstrated 512 Gb/s over 32 channels (about 16 Gb/s per channel) is well below that target. The 'scalable to hundreds of channels' statement is an authors' claim, not a measured result. The abstract also describes the comb source as a separate chip-based microresonator, so the result is not a pure silicon transceiver.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Setting the 1.6 Tb/s demand (from the grating-coupler review) beside a 512 Gb/s demonstration suggests a closer match than the evidence shows. The scaling statement is asserted, not demonstrated.
finding.supporting_excerpt: experimentally show aggregate single-fibre data transmission of 512 Gb s−1 across 32 independent wavelength channels. The demonstrated architecture is fundamentally scalable to hundreds of wavelength channels

finding.claim: S3 rests its 'around the weak electro-optic effect' narrative on one 2026 preprint. The preprint reports a single switch element, not a large array or system. The abstract gives no data on yield, long-term reliability, or the cumulative loss and crosstalk of a large switch fabric. The 20 nW figure is static power only, so dynamic and drive-electronics costs are not addressed. Large-scale switching is the stated motivation but is not demonstrated.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Element-level, not-yet-peer-reviewed results are used to support a platform-level conclusion. The abstract states the large-scale goal as a motivation, not a result.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The optical switch element exhibits an insertion loss of less than 1.5 dB with a low static power consumption of approx 20 nW at maximum actuation voltage.

finding.claim: S4 treats a single preprint as evidence that heterogeneous lithium tantalate is an 'active route'. The 'first integration without modifying the PDK' claim is the authors' own priority claim, not independently verified. The finding omits the caveat in the same abstract that lithium contamination complicates CMOS integration. It also omits that thin-film lithium niobate/tantalate is framed as an alternative to silicon modulators, which weakens the case for silicon itself at 1600ZR+ rates.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The finding is labelled verified_fact, but it reports only what a preprint claims. It leaves out the contamination risk and the implication that silicon-only modulators may fall short of emerging standards.
finding.supporting_excerpt: However, a persistent drawback of such platforms is the lithium contamination, which complicates integration with CMOS fabrication processes.

finding.claim: S10 says the gaps are 'component-level rather than system-level'. The cited visible/NIR review lists key component challenges but does not say system-level gaps are absent. S1's roadmap names integration and packaging bottlenecks as common problems. S10 also says 'both' extensions hinge on these gaps, yet only the visible/NIR paper is cited for it. The beyond-1.6 µm detector evidence comes from a different preprint, so S10 is an inference presented as verified fact.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract lists component challenges but makes no 'rather than system-level' comparison. The roadmap abstract names integration, circuit and packaging challenges, which are not purely component-level.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The key challenges are low-loss waveguides, efficient input/output coupling, sensitive detectors, and heterogeneous integration of lasers and modulators

finding.claim: S9 presents PbS colloidal quantum dots as an integrable route past 1.6 µm, based on one preprint. The 1.1 MHz bandwidth is orders of magnitude below datacom photodiode speeds, so it suits sensing and spectrometry, not high-speed links. The finding does not say this, and the 'verified_fact' label covers only reported device numbers. Reliability, yield and wafer-scale manufacturability are not addressed.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract positions the device for sensing around 2 µm. The 'scalability' claim rests on an 8-channel spectrometer, a small demonstration.
finding.supporting_excerpt: a bandwidth of 1.1 MHz under a -3 V bias

finding.claim: S7 lists entanglement purification as an emerging application but omits that the errors were simulated using reconfigurable on-chip circuits, not arising from real channel noise. The fidelity gain (0.71 to 0.82) was shown for a 20% bit-flip error. This is a first-demonstration preprint with a narrow test, not evidence of application readiness. The calibration paper is a method paper on a 6-phase-shifter chip.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The lab-scale, emulated-noise character of the quantum results is not stated in S7, though its 'low' severity partly reflects this.
finding.supporting_excerpt: To evaluate the purification performance, we simulate the bit-flip and phase-flip errors by reconfigurable circuits on chip.

finding.claim: The findings largely omit the on-chip light source, which is the most challenging silicon photonics component because of silicon's indirect bandgap. Lasers need III-V or other heterogeneous integration, adding process complexity. S1, S5, S6 and S10 imply a mainly silicon-foundry path, but several of the cited advances (lithium tantalate, quantum-dot detectors, Kerr comb sources, SiN waveguides) depend on non-silicon materials. That undercuts how much of the roadmap can be met with a silicon-only platform.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is a gap in coverage, not an error in any one finding. It matters for judging scaling to billions of units.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The most challenging aspect remains to be the on-chip laser source, whose performance is constrained by the indirect bandgap of silicon.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only titles and abstracts were reviewed; one abstract is truncated, so conclusions may be incomplete.
There are only 12 papers, mostly reviews and device-level demonstrations. They contain no market, cost, yield-at-volume or supply-chain data, so cost and single-supplier risks cannot be assessed.
Search coverage appears weighted toward device physics, with little on co-packaged optics, power consumption at system scale or competing technologies such as copper and VCSELs.
No arXiv preprints appear in this set, but several risk points rest on single abstracts.
One paper (src_bc726db42d) is dated 2026-08 and has zero citations; its results have not been independently assessed.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available, so claims were not checked against full-paper methods, data or limitations sections.
Several cited sources are arXiv preprints. I could not tell whether results were later revised or peer-reviewed.
No independent search for contradicting work on specific numbers was possible beyond the supplied 22 papers.
S1 and S2 are closely supported by their abstracts and were left unchallenged. S8 is already labelled an unverified claim and was not challenged further.
Some challenges are interpretive (ai_interpretation), reflecting judgement on framing and emphasis rather than quoted contradictions.

sources.title: STRUCTURES AND METHODS FOR INTEGRATED OPTICS MICROELECTROMECHANICAL SYSTEMS [US20260339027A1]
sources.organization: MENARD FRANCOIS, BRIERE JONATHAN, BERARD MARTIN
sources.abstract: [0000]    Silicon Photonics is a candidate technology for adding integrated optics functionality, either passive or active optical waveguides) to integrated circuits by leveraging the economies of scale of the CMOS microelectronics industry and using materials for the waveguide core such as silicon nitride (Si<X>N<Y>) and silicon oxynitride (SiO<X>N<1-X>) for example. Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) provide for movable platforms relative to the substrate allowing additional functionality to be added to a silicon circuit but also Silicon Photonics. Accordingly, by combining “fixed” waveguides formed upon a substrate with “movable” waveguides formed upon one or more movable or extendible platforms the inventors have established a series of Integrated Optics MEMS (IO-MEMS) elements based on Silicon Photonics. Such IO-MEMS include optical switches, optical attenuators, optical gates, optical switch matrices, configurable wavelength division multiplexer/demultiplexer devices, phase shifters, phase modulators and amplitude modulators exploiting suspended platforms and beams.

sources.title: OPTICAL INTERCONNECT MONITORING AND FAULT DETECTION IN DISTRIBUTED COMPUTING COMPONENTS [US20260322683A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A system for monitoring optical computing components is disclosed. The system may include processors and non-transitory computer-readable media comprising instructions. The system may receive optical measurements from optical interconnects internal to a distributed computing system, where the optical interconnects couple distributed computing components each having an associated optical communication device enabling optical communication at a package level. The system may receive performance metrics of the distributed computing components comprising workload activity, synchronization behavior, or thermal conditions. The system may input the optical measurements and performance metrics into an artificial intelligence model trained to predict potential faults. The system may determine a fault domain comprising a chiplet interface, an optical engine, a laser source, a coupler, or a reconfigurable optical path. The system may generate a message comprising a repair recommendation, an alert, or an automated corrective action based on the fault domain.

sources.title: CLOCK FORWARDING IN PACKAGED OPTICS LINKS [US20260312713A1]
sources.abstract: Conventional packaged optics systems recover clock from data signals using clock and data recovery circuitry, which introduces jitter. The recovered clock cannot perfectly track timing variations in the data signal because the recovery circuitry operates with finite bandwidth and response time. This timing misalignment reduces effective eye opening at the receiver and may require more powerful forward error correction schemes that consume additional power and introduce latency. The present disclosure addresses this problem by transmitting the clock on a dedicated wavelength channel through the same optical fiber as the data channels. Because the clock signal traverses the same optical medium and experiences similar propagation characteristics, the forwarded clock tracks jitter present in the data channels. This reduces effective jitter at the sampling instant and may eliminate gearbox circuitry otherwise required for rate conversion. These techniques may be applied to packaged optics architectures, including co-packaged optics and near-packaged optics configurations.

sources.title: Optoelectronic Devices Including Selectable Anode and Cathode Regions Able to Drive Coupled PMOS or NMOS Transistors in a Complementary Push-Pull Configuration [US20260301659A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Optoelectronic devices having simultaneously and independently addressable anode and cathode regions. They support a push-pull complementary transistor driving configuration that employs at least one PMOS transistor coupled to the p-type anode region and at least one NMOS transistor coupled to the n-type cathode region to drive each optoelectronic element in a complementary push-pull mode. Independent addressability of the cathode and anode is enabled by an electrically inactive p-type isolation region, which forms a depletion region with the n-type cathode to electrically isolate individual elements. The push-pull configuration provides enhanced switching speed, reduced static power dissipation, wider dynamic range, improved noise rejection, and greater design flexibility. The PMOS and NMOS transistors may be fabricated on a standard CMOS backplane wafer bonded to the optoelectronic element array, fully leveraging standard CMOS foundry capabilities for high-resolution micro-LED displays, detector arrays, data center optical interconnects, co-packaged optics, and optical transceiver arrays.

sources.abstract: Optical system and devices facilitating bidirectional, non-crossing optical node communications for high-speed, high bandwidth communication system architectures. The system includes an array of bi-directional (or even tri- or quad-directional) optical signal/light turning elements, each light turning element including one or more turning mirrors that can be inserted into an optical PCBs. Each light turning element of the array includes: a set of waveguide structures, each waveguide structure of said set for receiving and channeling optical signals; a set of internal light reflective surfaces, each internal light reflective surface associated with each waveguide structure, and one or more light focusing lenses disposed above said set of internal light reflective surfaces, each internal light reflective surface receiving optical signals through one light focusing lens for re-direction to a waveguide structure, or receiving optical signals from a waveguide structure for re-direction through the one light focusing lens.

sources.title: OPTICAL INTERCONNECT MODULE WITH TRANSVERSELY EXTENDED ALIGNMENT FEATURES [WO2026198422A1]
sources.abstract: An optical interconnect module that includes a carrier subassembly with transversely extended alignment features configured to match alignment features defined in opposed lateral faces of an optical subassembly is described. The transversely extended alignment features may be pillars and the matching alignment features may be grooves. The carrier subassembly includes electrooptic elements that are placed in electrical communication with other elements of the optical interconnect module by either wirebonds or flip-chip electrical connections. The optical subassembly may be an optical ferrule subassembly that supports a plurality of optical waveguides or an optical block configured to mate with an optical ferrule that supports a plurality of optical waveguides. The optical ferrule subassembly or optical ferrule may be attachable and detachable from the optical interconnect module.

sources.title: OPTICAL INTERCONNECT WITHIN 3D STACK OF WAFER SCALE COMPUTES [US20260287839A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Consistent with an aspect of the present disclosure, an optical interconnect layer is provided that provides a high speed, low crosstalk optical connection between stacked wafer scale circuitry. The optical interconnect layer includes optoelectronic devices, such as LEDs on side and other optoelectronic devices, such as photodiodes, on the other side. Optical signals emitted by the LEDs may, in one example, be transmitted on optical fibers extending between the LEDs and photodiodes. In another example, light pipes including a transmissive material, such as polyimide, are embedded in a housing, and, in a further example, lenses are provided to focus light output by the LEDs onto the photodiodes. In an additional example, optical paths, such as optical fibers or light pipes, carrying the optical signals are included in conduits, whereby a coolant may be circulated between the conduits to thereby absorb heat generated by the wafer scale circuitry.

sources.title: CO-PACKAGED OPTICS STRUCTURE WITH OPTICAL CONNECTORS HAVING WAVEGUIDE STRESS RELIEF FEATURES [US20260287830A1]
sources.abstract: A connector structure for coupling optical signals to a semiconductor device includes a connector body comprising a recessed portion extending from a first side of the connector body to a second side of the connector body, an optical waveguide structure comprising one or more waveguides, the optical waveguide structure being positioned in the recessed portion of the connector body and extending from the first side of the connector body and out through the second side of the connector body, and a lid positioned over the optical waveguide structure, the lid securing the optical waveguide structure in the recessed portion of the connector body, the lid having a first edge and a second edge, the first edge of the lid being proximate to the first side of the connector body, the second edge of the lid being offset from an edge at the second side of the connector body.

sources.title: Optical Switch with Fast Switching and Fast Transceiver Acquisition [US20260292375A1]
sources.abstract: This disclosure presents systems and methods for an optical circuit switch (OCS), optical burst switch (OBS), and hybrid OBS (HOBS) featuring microsecond-range reconfiguration times—critical for modern AI/ML workloads demanding both low latency and high bandwidth. By combining fast switching elements (e.g., silicon photonics) with burst-mode transceivers that reduce acquisition from seconds to microseconds, the proposed architectures enable efficient data center interconnects. The design coordinates switch reconfiguration and transceiver lock-in through in-band or out-of-band control, minimizing overhead to under ten percent of each burst's duration. Additional optimizations—such as buffering packet headers, using a second wavelength for control signals, and employing partial DSP training—further boost performance while reducing power consumption. These fast optical switches support both short, frequent bursts (scale-up) and large, stable flows (scale-out), delivering high-throughput, low-latency connections suitable for AI/ML clusters, HPC environments, and other dynamic data center applications.

sources.title: HIGH-PRECISION DETACHABLE OPTICAL INTERCONNECT [WO2026190791A1]
sources.abstract: Some examples of the present disclosure are directed to a detachable connector for a co-packaged optics (CPO) device. The detachable connector may include a kinematic mount, where the kinematic mount includes a first kinematic interface configured to engage a corresponding kinematic interface of the CPO device. In some examples, the kinematic mount is configured for repeated detachment and attachment with substantially identical alignment between the detachable connector and the CPO device within a predetermined sub-micron tolerance. Furthermore, in an attached state, the kinematic mount may be configured to provide an optical transmission path between the CPO device and the detachable connector, where a transmission loss along the optical transmission path remains within a predetermined threshold tolerance.

sources.title: DEVICES AND METHODS FOR DETACHABLE COUPLING OF CO-PACKAGED OPTICAL CONNECTORS [US20260276925A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Some embodiments of the present disclosure are directed to a method for manufacturing detachable electronic modules. The method may include forming a detachable connector package by aligning a plurality of detachable connectors with respect to one another at a first alignment tolerance, wherein each of the plurality of detachable connectors comprises a first kinematic interface, and  providing a co-packaged optics (CPO) device, the CPO device comprising a plurality of photonics integrated circuits (PICs), wherein each PIC of the plurality of PICs is coupled to a CPO connector comprising a second kinematic interface. The method may further include attaching the detachable connector package to a co-packaged optics (CPO) device by engaging each first kinematic interface with a corresponding second kinematic interface such that each of the plurality of detachable connectors aligns with each of the plurality of PICs within a predetermined sub-micron tolerance.

sources.title: MULTI-LEVEL ALIGNMENT SYSTEM FOR HIGH-DENSITY OPTICAL INTERCONNECTS [WO2026190792A1]
sources.abstract: Some examples are directed to a multi-level alignment system for high-density optical interconnects includes a detachable connector package comprising multiple optical connectors, each with a kinematic interface, and a co-packaged optics (CPO) device comprising photonics integrated circuits (PICs) with corresponding mounting elements. The system employs multi-level self-alignment including package-level rough alignment, individual connector alignment, and functional fine alignment at sub-micron tolerances. A force application mechanism maintains engagement between kinematic interfaces during attached states. Methods include aligning detachable connectors with respect to one another at a first tolerance, aligning each connector to a corresponding PIC at a second tolerance, and engaging kinematic interfaces to achieve sub-micron precision alignment, enabling optical signal propagation between fiber array units and PICs without manual optical performance monitoring.

sources.title: MULTI-CONNECTION OPTICAL FIBER ASSEMBLY [US20260276906A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    An optical fiber assembly comprises a plurality of first connectors each having a first plurality of optical channels and a plurality of second connectors for connection with a Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) switch, each having a second plurality of optical channels. The first connectors are connected with the second connectors via a plurality of optical fibers, such that each first connector is connected with all of the second connectors. The optical fiber assembly includes twice as many first connectors as second connectors, and consequently each second connector includes twice as many optical fiber connections as each first connector.

draft.summary: Research on silicon photonics is growing: publications rose 12.4% in 2025 and are up 28.8% so far in 2026, so momentum is still building [S1, S6]. The commercial evidence is strongest for AI data-centre interconnects and co-packaged optics. Company filings describe product portfolios, M&A and a test and manufacturing supply chain forming [M1, M2, M3, M4, M5], and recent patent filings cluster on co-packaged optics connectors and thermal management [P1, P2]. Several of the cited technical advances depend on non-silicon materials such as III-V lasers, silicon nitride, lithium tantalate and quantum dots, so the winning platform may be hybrid [R1, R6, C8]. Non-datacom uses such as sensing and quantum are early, with narrow preprint evidence [R8, C7]. Scaling from millions to billions of units is unproven [S1, R4]. Related stocks are in sharp, volatile drawdowns, and some of the demand evidence comes from unverified social posts [T7, X1, X5].
draft.plain_summary: Silicon photonics uses light instead of electricity to move data on chips, and it matters most for the fast links inside AI data centres. Research and company activity are both growing, and some products already ship. The main thing that could hold it back is making it in far larger volumes, because the light sources and some other parts still need materials other than silicon, which adds cost and complexity.

themes.name: Co-packaged optics and AI data-centre interconnect

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Data-centre transceivers are the main current volume use [R4]. Company filings show commercial portfolios and acquisitions around silicon photonics and CPO [M1, M2, M3]. Social-media earnings summaries point to strong AI optical demand [X5], but they are secondary and unverified, and the related stocks are in steep, volatile drawdowns [T7].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Patent filings on detachable CPO connectors, thermal management and fibre routing suggest industry effort is going into serviceability and density [P1, P2, P3]. A supporting test ecosystem is forming [M4, M5]. Whether CPO scales depends on solving packaging, fabrication and thermal-crosstalk limits [S1, R2, R3]. Evidence on actual customer adoption of CPO is thin.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The roadmap asks for growth from millions to billions of units, but this is described as unproven [S1, R4]. The lab demonstrations for AI links, such as the Kerr comb link, are far below 1.6 Tb/s targets and are not pure silicon [C2, R5]. The evidence cannot say who wins at this horizon.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: AI bandwidth demand keeps outpacing electrical links [X3]. CPO moves into volume, and the packaging and connector filings turn into serviceable products [P1, P2]. Foundries and optical component makers keep reporting strong growth [X5, X1], and the consolidation and acquisitions seen so far continue [M2, M3].

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Silicon photonics stays the main platform for data-centre optics. It grows with AI infrastructure spending, and supply-chain participants (test, packaging, coating) benefit [M4, M5]. Progress is gradual and limited by lasers, thermal effects and fabrication variability [R1, R2, R3].

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Packaging, laser integration and yield problems slow the move to billions of units [S1, R4]. Alternative or hybrid platforms such as InP, silicon nitride and thin-film lithium niobate or tantalate take key functions [R6, C4]. Related stocks are already volatile and in drawdown, so sentiment could stay weak [T7].

themes.name: Hybrid and heterogeneous integration for light sources and modulators

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Lasers still depend on III-V or other heterogeneous integration [R1]. The modulator and MEMS advances are single preprints and lack yield, reliability and system-scale data [C3, C4]. Near-term commercial signals are limited to filings from small firms licensing materials [M6] and a coating-equipment supplier for InP lasers [M5].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Silicon's weak electro-optic effect drives research into alternative materials and MEMS [S2, S3, S4]. Foundry-compatible integration is claimed but not independently verified. Lithium contamination complicates CMOS integration, and thin-film niobate or tantalate is framed as an alternative to silicon modulators [C4]. Evidence is too thin to say which approach prevails.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Several advances rely on non-silicon materials, so the winning platform may be hybrid [R6, C8]. Isolators and polarization management are unresolved integration issues [R7]. The evidence does not support a firm view at this horizon.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Foundry-compatible heterogeneous integration of modulators, lasers and MEMS switches proves manufacturable, which removes silicon's main limits while keeping the existing foundry ecosystem [S3, S4].

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Hybrid integration progresses incrementally. Silicon remains the base platform but depends on III-V, silicon nitride and other materials for demanding functions [R6, R1].

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Integration complexity, contamination, yield and reliability problems keep these approaches at lab scale, or non-silicon platforms capture the value [C3, C4, R6].

themes.name: Emerging non-datacom applications: sensing, visible/NIR and quantum

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Evidence is early: a conference paper on composites sensing with no cost or incumbent comparison [R8], a simulated entanglement purification preprint [C7], and a quantum-dot detector with 1.1 MHz bandwidth suited to sensing, not datacom [C6]. No market evidence of customer adoption was found.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Research is extending platforms to 380-1100 nm and beyond 1.6 µm [S5, S9], but the visible platforms are silicon nitride and aluminum oxide, not silicon [C1]. Component gaps include low-loss waveguides, coupling, detectors and laser integration [S10], though system-level gaps are not ruled out [C5]. Sensing and computing products are described as 'around the corner' [R4].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Quantum and design-automation uses are research threads with low-confidence evidence [S7, S8, C7]. The evidence does not support a view on commercial outcomes.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Platform extensions to visible, NIR and mid-IR wavelengths open sensing, biosensing and quantum markets, helped by design automation and foundry access [S5, S8, S9].

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: These uses remain niche and research-led. Much of the visible-range progress comes from silicon nitride and aluminum oxide rather than silicon [C1, R8].

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Cost, reliability and incumbent technologies prevent volume adoption, and the quantum and sensing results stay narrow demonstrations [C7, C6, R8].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Cost and performance comparisons against incumbent fibre sensors, and manufacturing data for quantum-dot detectors
